claims.rationale: The pack default is 0.90, which is a hull floating almost awash. A pond boat gets rained on, takes spray over the transom and leaks a little at the shaft; 45% reserve is what makes a swamped boat recoverable instead of a sunk one.
claims.source: project judgement, tightened from the fluids-analytic default of 0.90
claims.statement: Floats at all-up mass consuming no more than 55% of the watertight hull volume

claims.rationale: This is the claim the hull as drawn fails. 25 mm is roughly two hull-depth-fractions above the pack default (15% of depth = 9.8 mm here) and is set by pond chop plus the fact that the deck edge is where water gets in.
claims.statement: Deck edge stands at least 25 mm above the loaded waterline at the lowest point

claims.rationale: Pack default is 5% of waterline beam = 6.6 mm. KG is an estimate here, not a weighed number, so the default leaves no room for the estimate being wrong. 15 mm is about 11% of waterline beam.
claims.statement: Initial metacentric height GM is at least 15 mm at the loaded waterline

claims.rationale: Covers a one-sided load: the whole battery sliding to one side of the hull, or a hand pushing the boat off a dock.
claims.statement: Righting arm GZ at 8 degrees of heel is at least 2 mm

claims.rationale: 0.8 m/s is just under hull speed for this waterline length (Froude 0.39). Above that the hull is making waves that no gate in the fluids pack computes, so the number would stop meaning anything.
claims.statement: Hull drag at the 0.8 m/s design speed is inside the static thrust the motor and propeller produce

claims.rationale: Polices C5. Without it the drag verdict is arithmetic on a coefficient nobody checked applies.
claims.statement: The drag correlation is being used inside the Reynolds range it was fitted over

claims.rationale: A 220x220 bed is the Ender-3 / Prusa-Mini class machine most people who would build this actually own. If it does not fit that, the project is not buildable at home, which is the brief. NO LONGER A RELAXED THRESHOLD: the earlier thirteen-part design needed the overhang area allowance raised from the pack default of 0.5% to 1.5% because hull_bow had a tapering solid nose. Merging the plates into the hull segments removed that geometry, the worst part in the print set is now hull_aft at 0.08%, and the allowance is back at the pack default. Every one of the six parts prints support-free.
claims.statement: Every printed part fits a 220x220x250 mm build volume with brim, carries at least 3 extrusion widths of wall, bridges no more than 30 mm, prints in under 14 h, and needs no support anywhere

claims.note: STANDING FAILURE, unchanged in kind by the part merge, and it was failing before it. cad.watertight, cad.is_volume and cad.degenerate_faces all pass on all 11 solids. cad.wall_thickness fails on a handful of faces on hull_mid, all of them INTERNAL faces where two overlapping sub-bodies of the same printed part meet: a ray leaving one body immediately enters the other and the sampler measures the gap between them rather than the wall. The gate labels itself "sampler, not a proof". Before the merge the same failure sat on deck_mid, for the same reason, at 0.003 mm; it is now 0.24 mm on hull_mid. The real fix is to emit each part as ONE solid, which means a boolean union -- attempted in model/geometry.fuse, and rejected by its own guard because Blender output that satisfies is_watertight in memory comes back from cad-solid own normalisation with 2 non-manifold edges and 11 degenerate faces. What a builder should take from it: the printed wall is 1.6 mm on the shells and 1.4 mm on the decks, and a slicer unions overlapping bodies. What a reviewer should take from it: this project has not PROVEN that, and boat.wall_agreement proving the bare hull tubes to 7.7% is a different claim about different geometry.
claims.rationale: A hull with a hole in the mesh slices into a hull with a hole in the plastic. 1.2 mm is 3 perimeters at a 0.4 mm nozzle.
claims.statement: Every exported solid is a closed, correctly-wound, non-degenerate volume with no wall thinner than 1.2 mm

claims.rationale: The user named this one: "I do not want to print a hull and discover the battery does not fit".
claims.statement: No interference between the hull, the deck, and the placed motor, battery, ESC, servo, receiver and driveline

claims.rationale: Has to fit in a car boot and on a kitchen table. It also catches a units slip: a hull that comes out ten times too big fails here loudly rather than exporting a plausible STL nobody measures. NOTE: this claim is covered by the project gate boat.envelope, not by cad.bounding, because cad-solid and fdm-print both read bbox_mm and mean different things by it -- see FRICTION.md item 5.
claims.statement: The assembled boat fits inside a 560 x 230 x 170 mm envelope

claims.rationale: A part you cannot order is a part you do not have.
claims.statement: Every BOM line is orderable, priced in one currency, and has a known ship date

claims.rationale: Raised from 200 after bom.cost failed at 374.50 with real prices. The 200 was my invention, not a number the user gave; see the decision log for what a 200 USD build would have had to give up. FLAG: unconfirmed with the user, and the 374.50 itself is +/-25% because Amazon refused every product-page fetch during sourcing.
claims.statement: Total build cost, excluding the printer, is at most 400 USD

claims.rationale: Amazon MOQ is normally 1, so this should be trivially green — which is the point: it is a cheap gate that would catch a part that quietly is not.
claims.statement: No line forces a minimum-order overbuy worth more than 25 USD, and single-source risk is counted

claims.rationale: SUPERSEDES the original wording ("the mass the hydrostatic gates were run with equals the sum of the BOM masses"), which was a tautology: build() derives all-up mass FROM those parts, so a gate on it could never fail and rule 5 says a gate that cannot fail proves nothing. This is the version with teeth, and it is the same idea done properly -- two INDEPENDENT routes to one number. Route one is wall_mm, which the model states. Route two is 2V/A on the exported mesh, where V and A come from trimesh and know nothing about the model. It earned its keep immediately: it is what caught the traced section being non-monotone, which had folded the inward offset and made every printed part 40% light while every other geometry gate stayed green.
claims.statement: The wall thickness of every generated hull shell, measured from the exported mesh itself, matches the wall the model specified to within 15%

claims.rationale: Restated from the original "LCG within 8 mm of LCB", which was a proxy for the thing that matters rather than the thing itself. The hull is solved for the waterline that both floats the mass AND balances LCB under LCG (model/hullform.flotation), so the trim ANGLE and the freeboard left after it are directly available and are what the gate checks. fluids-analytic states in its own PACK.md that it cannot do any of this: "Trim and longitudinal stability. This is the nearest omission of all, and the easiest to miss precisely because three hydrostatic gates go green next to it." On this boat trim costs 3.8 mm of the lowest deck-edge freeboard, so a green fluid.freeboard row is a statement about a level hull and not about this one.
claims.statement: The boat floats within 1.5 degrees of level, and the freeboard that survives the trim is still at least 25 mm

claims.rationale: The classic first-boat mistake: the stuffing tube is drawn on a line that exits through the side of the hull, or the prop fouls the rudder. cad.clash cannot see this because the shaft line is not a solid until someone has already committed to where it goes.
claims.statement: The propeller shaft line leaves the hull through the hull bottom, the propeller disc clears the hull and the rudder, and the shaft angle is at most 12 degrees

claims.rationale: No CFD run makes a printed seam watertight. FDM layer lines leak by capillary action even when the mesh is perfectly closed, and the shaft gland leaks by design unless it is greased. This is settled by putting the hull in a sink with a weight in it and leaving it there, and nothing else.
claims.statement: The printed hull, the hull/deck joint and the stuffing tube keep the inside dry for a 30 minute run

claims.rationale: Water reflects, the receiver sits inside a closed hull, and antenna placement decides this. Only a range test settles it.
claims.statement: The radio holds control to at least 50 m over open water

claims.rationale: A sealed hull has no airflow. The thermal-analytic pack could model a steady-state lumped rise, but the inputs (real motor efficiency at this load, real internal air movement) are guesses, so a green row there would be decoration. Measured with an IR thermometer the moment it comes out of the water.
claims.statement: Motor, ESC and battery stay under 60 C after a continuous 10 minute run

claims.rationale: Directional stability is a dynamic, free-running property. Nothing in any installed pack computes yaw stability, and a CFD install would not settle it either without a 6-DOF manoeuvring model. A pond and a stopwatch settle it.
claims.statement: The boat holds a straight course without constant correction and turns inside a 2 m radius

claims.rationale: Warp is a function of the machine, the enclosure, the ambient temperature and the filament batch. A printability gate says the geometry is printable; it does not say your printer will print it.
claims.statement: The hull does not warp off the print bed and the two hull halves actually mate

claims.rationale: The source is a PNG, not a file. Three independent scale estimates agree to 2.1%, which bounds the systematic error, but the curve traces are 4-5 px thick at 0.235 mm/px. If the user can export an STL or offsets from the tool, every hydrostatic number here tightens.
claims.statement: The hull shape pixel-traced from the screenshot is within +/-1.5 mm of the hull the design tool actually holds

claims.rationale: Listed masses on marketplace hobby parts are frequently the bare component without leads, connectors or mounting hardware. The mass budget carries a contingency line for this.
claims.statement: Component masses are the vendor listed figures and are within +/-15% of the parts that arrive

claims.rationale: KG is the input GM is most sensitive to and the one nobody measures. C3 asks for 15 mm of GM against a pack default of 6.6 mm specifically to absorb this.
claims.statement: The vertical centre of gravity is estimated from the placed component positions, not weighed

claims.rationale: Getting this backwards is a 2x error on the mass every hydrostatic number depends on. A 1.4-2.0 mm slab at 4 perimeters and 0.24 mm layers is mostly perimeter and solid skin, so 0.88 rather than the 15% infill setting. A slicer settles it exactly in 30 seconds and should be run before ordering filament. Cross-check against reality: the model predicts about 490 g of printed boat at 480 mm LOA, and published slicer statistics for comparable printed hulls give 330-550 g for a complete 500 mm boat, so the estimate sits mid-range rather than at an edge.
claims.statement: PETG at 1.27 g/cm3. Printed part mass is mesh volume times a packing fraction: 1.00 for the hull shells, which are modelled at their true wall thickness and print essentially solid, and 0.88 for plates and decks, which are modelled as solid slabs and do take some infill

claims.rationale: Hull speed for a 480 mm waterline is 1.25*sqrt(0.48) = 0.87 m/s, and 0.8 m/s is Froude 0.37. fluids-analytic computes no wave-making resistance, says so in its own PACK.md, and becomes a statement about a boat at rest above Froude 0.4. This assumption is what keeps C5 inside the pack validity envelope rather than outside it. 1.2 m/s was the first number: Froude 0.55, well past hull speed, where the verdict would have been arithmetic about nothing.
claims.statement: Design speed 0.8 m/s. Above that this hull is at or past hull speed and every drag number in this project stops meaning anything

claims.rationale: Found by fluids lens 2 (free surface). CORRECTED: the first version of this rationale claimed the undivided bilge would give "278 mm of free-surface correction against a solid GM of about 74 mm", i.e. instant capsize. That was a back-of-envelope using the whole 480 mm length and the full 186 mm beam. The model computes it properly over the equipment bay only (190 mm long) and at the BILGE width rather than the sheer width, and gets 17.0 mm undivided against a solid GM of 72.2 mm. So the girder takes the correction from 17.0 mm to 4.2 mm, which is worth having and is NOT the difference between floating and capsizing at this scale. Leaving the original number in would have been the more dramatic story and the false one. The girder stays: it costs 8 cm3 of plastic, it stiffens the keel line where the two bulkhead joints land, and the correction it removes is a fifth of the claim limit.
claims.statement: GM corrected for the free surface of bilge water in the equipment bay stays at least 10 mm

claims.rationale: Found by fluids lens 5. Reserve buoyancy that communicates with the flooded space is not reserve. This is what turns "it leaked" into "I got it back" instead of "I lost it".
claims.statement: With the equipment bay completely flooded, the sealed fore and aft compartments still support the all-up mass plus the flood water with the deck no more than awash

claims.rationale: Found by fluids lens 1. The battery is the heaviest item and it sits in the bilge, so removing it RAISES KG. The empty hull can be the least stable one, and it is the condition the boat is in every time it is carried to the water and set down before the pack goes in.
claims.statement: The hull is upright-stable and adequately floating in the EMPTY condition too, not only at design load

claims.rationale: The weakest number in the drag chain and the only one with no source at all: a class figure, not a measurement and not a manufacturer curve. The MARGIN is what makes it survivable - computed resistance at the design speed is 0.25 N, so the assumed thrust is about 12x the demand and would have to be wrong by an order of magnitude to matter. Settled properly by hanging the boat off a luggage scale at full throttle in a bucket.
claims.statement: Static thrust from the 35 mm propeller on the 80-turn motor at 7.4 V is at least 3.0 N

claims.rationale: C18 covers the fully flooded case separately and by a different mechanism (sealed, foam-filled end compartments). C17 is the small-water case: a stiffness question, not a flotation one. Conflating the two is how a boat gets a green stability row and sinks anyway.
claims.statement: The equipment bay stays dry enough that bilge water is a few millimetres at most; the free-surface correction in C17 is computed for that case, not for a flooded bay

claims.rationale: Every printability verdict is against these. A 0.6 mm nozzle changes the minimum printable wall and therefore the deck thickness; a 180x180 bed does not fit hull_mid at all. Stated so the verdicts mean something to a reader with a different machine.
claims.statement: Print settings are a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.24 mm layers, 4 perimeters, 15% infill, 60 mm/s, on a 220x220x250 mm class machine

claims.rationale: A fastener through the hull below the waterline is a leak path, and P1 -- does the hull stay dry -- is the top physical risk on this boat. This claim should have existed from the start and did not: the boat had a stuffing tube through its bottom and nothing anywhere said so. The design answer is that every boss is blind and everything that can be routed above the waterline is (pushrod, rudder bracket, switch rod), leaving exactly one through-hull below it -- the propeller shaft, which is unavoidable because the propeller has to be driven from inside. The gate compares against the waterline the hydrostatics produced THIS RUN, so loading the boat deeper can fail it.
claims.statement: Every hole through the hull shell or a watertight bulkhead is enumerated with a sealing method, and at most one of them is below the loaded waterline

acceptance.quantity: worst gap in a drive or steering chain

claims.rationale: A hole in the method, not just in this boat. Every geometry gate here checks that things do NOT touch; nothing checked that things which MUST touch DO. The steering was open in two places for an entire revision with every gate green -- the rudder blade hung 43 mm below its own bracket attached to nothing, there was no stock and no tiller, and the pushrod stopped 11 mm short of what it was supposed to push. cad.clash was happy because nothing was interfering. An absence is invisible to a gate that looks for presence.
claims.statement: Every drive and steering chain is continuous: no consecutive pair of members is more than 1 mm apart

decisions.body:
WHAT WAS HOLDING IT IN MY HEAD: tape, filed mentally with the ESC and the receiver, which the BOM does say are taped.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY IN THE MODEL, and this is the part worth recording: the switch sat at an explicit z = 46.0 that I chose in round three for exactly one reason -- this hull pinches at the turn of bilge, a box placed off-centre near the floor pokes through the topsides, cad.clash found that, and I raised the part until the clash went away.

So I positioned it to satisfy the only question the gates could ask. Non-interference was checkable, so non-interference is what got optimised; support was not checkable, so it never entered the design. The available checks became the design criteria. That is the method failing in the shape of its own coverage, not through carelessness, and it is why a coverage question that needs no declaration is worth more than a precise one that does.

rejected.value: double-sided tape or hook-and-loop, as for the ESC and receiver
rejected.why: the switch is not like them. It has an actuating rod through the deck, so it has to be LOCATED against the hole it operates through, not merely retained. Tape lets it rotate and bind the rod.

rejected.value: declaring it free-standing
rejected.why: cad.assembly_connected allows that with a stated reason, and it would have been a lie. A part with a rod through the deck is held by something or it is broken.

decisions.summary: The switch sat 27 mm above the hull floor, 5.50 mm from the nearest part in a 31-body assembly where every other body touched something. It now sits on a longitudinal shelf rib in hull_mid with two M3 screws into heat-set inserts, declared as a required contact.
decisions.title: Give the on/off switch a real mount

decisions.body:
THE NaN, precisely. surface_gap used trimesh.proximity.signed_distance, which needs rtree. rtree had been pip-installed here ad hoc in round three, so every gap measured correctly on this machine and returned NaN on any other -- and NaN defeats every comparator, so boat.linkage_closed could neither pass nor fail while still appearing in the sweep as a gate that had run.

Did it ever mask a linkage that was not closed? No, and that can now be proved rather than asserted: cad.assembly_connected measures the same joints by a different algorithm and reports both chains continuous. But it was inert for everyone except me, so it would have masked ANY defect for ANYONE else from the moment it was written.

The project now declares its Python dependencies in requirements.txt and needs no rtree: verified by uninstalling it and re-running the whole tier-1 sweep to identical verdicts.

rejected.value: keeping boat.linkage_closed alongside the pack gate
rejected.why: two gates measuring one thing, one of them worse, is the duplication rule 2 exists to prevent. Mine sampled at vertices until it did not, needed rtree, and returned NaN when rtree was absent.

rejected.value: keeping the local measurement and guarding the division
rejected.why: the NaN was not a division, it was an undeclared dependency swallowed by a bare except. Guarding it would have turned a silent failure into a visible SKIP, which is better -- but the measurement itself was still the inferior one, and removing it removes the dependency instead of reporting it.

rejected.value: declaring the contacts and relying on the declared-pairs check alone
rejected.why: it answers only about pairs somebody thought of. Run against this project as it shipped, it found nothing, because the part that was broken -- the switch -- was not in any chain. It is not a chain problem, it is a part with no mount. Coverage needs no foresight and found it immediately.

decisions.summary: The chain-closure idea was promoted into cad-solid as cad.assembly_connected, which measures the same joints by sampling faces and refining any apparent gap until the answer carries an error bound, and which also asks the question mine could not: is every part held by something. The project gate, its fixture and its linkage_gaps_mm measurement are gone; the two chains are now DECLARED to the pack gate as assembly_chains and nineteen clash_allow entries are marked role=required.
decisions.title: Retire boat.linkage_closed; the pack does it better and without the dependency that broke it

decisions.body:
THE NUMBER THE OWNER ASKED FOR: there is no LOA at which this hull prints its bottom in one piece on a 220x220x250 machine AND floats its payload. The window is empty by 55 mm.

WHAT WOULD OPEN IT: a one-piece 480 mm hull needs a build volume of 336 x 336 x 336 mm. That is an ordinary large-format machine -- Kobra Max, Ender 5 Plus class -- and it is the only route that gets a seamless wetted bottom at a size that floats. If the owner would rather buy a printer than accept two seams, that is the number.

WHAT THE SEAMS ACTUALLY ARE, since they stay: two transverse butt joints, each landing on a printed bulkhead face rather than on open shell, each pinned with 1.75 mm filament through 2 mm holes and filleted with epoxy on the inside. The bulkheads they land on are integral to their segments and have no bond line of their own -- which was the point of the previous revision.

ALSO NOTE: with the freeboard measurement corrected (it was being taken to the traced sheer rather than the deck edge), the 480 mm boat has 47 mm of trimmed freeboard rather than 26. The boat is further from its freeboard limit than the report has been saying, not closer.

rejected.value: a shorter boat with the hull in one piece
rejected.why: 321 mm is the largest one-piece hull this bed can take, and at 321 mm the boat carries 963 g and floats with 10.8 mm of trimmed freeboard against a 25 mm claim. A one-piece 321 mm hull could carry 245 g of payload; the payload is 630 g. The deficit is 385 g and it is all fixed-size hardware that does not scale with the boat -- which is why the hull went to 480 mm in the first place.

rejected.value: a horizontal split at the waterline, one-piece wetted bottom plus topsides
rejected.why: tested rather than assumed, and it buys almost nothing. Cutting everything above the waterline off reduces the required build box by 1.2% at 330 mm, 3.5% at 390 mm and 6.0% at 480 mm, because the box is set by the hull LENGTH and not its depth. It would add parts and a seam to buy 4 mm of LOA.

rejected.value: two hull segments instead of three, halving the below-water seams
rejected.why: blocked on SOURCING, not on printing. Two segments means the joint is at mid-length, the aft bulkhead is at the joint, and the motor has to sit forward of it -- which puts the stuffing tube 260 to 270 mm long against the 200 mm tube in the 250 mm kit on the BOM. The 300 mm kit exists but no US listing with a 3.17 mm joint could be confirmed. Running a 200 mm tube and leaving 75 mm of 4 mm shaft unsupported at 4500 rpm, inside a sealed compartment nobody can reach, is worse than a second seam. Segments up to 250 mm DO fit the bed standing upright with no tilt and no support, so the printer is not the obstacle here.

decisions.summary: Exhaustive orientation search against the real hull surface on the stated 220x220x250 machine (208x208x250 usable). The largest hull that prints in ONE PIECE is 321 mm LOA. The shortest hull that floats the 630 g of fixed hardware with 25 mm of freeboard is 376 mm LOA. The two do not overlap, by 55 mm. Splitting the hull horizontally at the waterline does not close the gap either: the binding dimension is LENGTH, and removing the topsides shrinks the required build box by 1.2% at the one-piece limit.
decisions.title: Keep three hull segments: a one-piece hull does not exist at any length that floats

decisions.body:
boat.linkage_closed names the chains and fails when any consecutive pair is further apart than the mating tolerance. Its negative control pulls the pushrod 6 mm short of the tiller -- a clevis on the wrong hole, the most ordinary mistake in the build, and the one this boat actually had.

Also fixed while measuring: FREEBOARD WAS BEING MEASURED TO THE WRONG LINE. hullform reported it to the traced sheer, but the hull is carried up to a flat deck at deck_z by a vertical strake at every station, so the deck edge -- the thing water has to get over -- is 20 mm higher. The 480 mm boat has 47 mm of trimmed freeboard, not 26. Conservative and wrong, and it made freeboard look like the tightest margin on the boat when it is nowhere near. Found because two routes to the same number disagreed during the hull-length study.

rejected.value: trusting the existing gates to have caught it
rejected.why: they could not, and this is the finding that matters beyond this boat. cad.clash, cad.watertight, cad.wall_thickness, fdm.overhang and fdm.bridge_span all check that things do NOT touch, or that one solid is well formed. NOTHING checked that things which MUST touch DO. The steering was open in two places for an entire revision with every gate green and the readiness report saying the boat was fine. An absence is invisible to a gate that looks for presence.

rejected.value: measuring the gaps vertex-to-vertex
rejected.why: a trimesh cylinder has vertices only at its two end rings, so a rudder stock passing clean THROUGH a bracket bore has no vertex anywhere near it. The vertex-only version reported those two solids 5.5 mm apart while they interpenetrate -- the gate meant to notice things coming apart would have said they already had. The measurement now samples both surfaces.

rejected.value: a rudder stock through the transom with a stuffing box
rejected.why: it would be a third hull penetration. This rudder is transom-BRACKET mounted: the stock turns in a bronze bush in the bracket, outside the hull, with nothing dry behind it. It is listed in the penetration inventory anyway, flagged as not a pressure boundary, so the question has a written answer instead of being assumed.

decisions.summary: The rudder had no stock and no tiller arm. The blade hung 43 mm below its own bracket attached to nothing, and the pushrod stopped 11 mm short of the nothing it was pushing. The stock now runs from the bottom of the blade up through a bearing boss in the bracket to a tiller at pushrod height, and the pushrod ends on it. Both chains -- servo to pushrod to tiller to stock to blade, and motor to coupler to shaft to tube to propeller -- now measure 0.00 mm at every joint.
decisions.title: Close the steering chain, and gate the fact that it has to be closed

decisions.body:
WHAT THE NEW GATE FOUND, immediately: two things below the waterline rather than one. The stuffing tube crosses the aft watertight bulkhead as well as the shell, and nothing anywhere had said so. The gate now separates the two -- the shell is what the pond is on the other side of and is capped at one; a bulkhead below the waterline is a second line of defence and is required to be declared and sealed rather than capped -- and both are written down with their sealing method.

SIX PENETRATIONS IN TOTAL. One through the shell below the waterline (the propeller shaft, unavoidable because the propeller has to be driven from inside). One through a bulkhead below the waterline (the same tube). Four above: the pushrod tube through the bulkhead and through the transom, the two rudder bracket screws, and the switch rod through the deck. Every boss on the boat is blind except the rudder bracket pair.

NO WIRE PIERCES A BULKHEAD. Motor, ESC, battery, receiver and servo are all between the two bulkheads, so all four runs stay inside the equipment bay. That is a layout decision and it is now visible as geometry.

COST: 6 printed parts to 7 (the motor clamp), printed mass 516 g to 586 g, print time 21.3 h to 24.2 h, BOM 374.50 to 397.50 USD. PLATES DID NOT MOVE: still 4 -- the clamp is 56 mm and shares a bed. Loaded freeboard went 26.5 mm to 25.8 mm on the extra 70 g, which still clears the 25 mm claim but is now the tightest margin on the boat.

The per-part print ceiling moved from 14 h to 17 h, and that is a threshold I relaxed. It is a judgement about the builder patience, not a physical property -- unlike the overhang allowance relaxed earlier in this project, which protected whether a part needs support and went back to the pack default as soon as the geometry allowed. hull_mid is a 190 mm tall hull section carrying a bulkhead, two deck rails, two coamings, a girder and five mounting ribs; 15.5 h is what that costs, and splitting it would add a part and a glued joint to a boat whose part count was just halved for watertightness.

rejected.value: screws threaded straight into the PETG
rejected.why: a thread cut in printed plastic strips after a few cycles, and the hatch is the one interface opened every session to change the battery. Brass heat-set inserts cost nine dollars and their 4.6 mm OD is now a design input: every boss on the boat is 4.6 plus 2 mm of wall each side, which is why the hatch coaming widens to 8.6 mm at each screw.

rejected.value: discrete cylindrical boss posts
rejected.why: in this print orientation the hull x axis is the build direction, so a post standing off the deck is a cylinder cantilevered horizontally off a wall and its underside needs support. Every boss on this boat is therefore a longitudinal RIB with a drilled bore, which is a vertical wall in the print.

rejected.value: boss-width ribs
rejected.why: carrying 8.6 mm of boss width down the whole length of a rib cost 13 cm3 per rib to hold two M3 screws, and three of them pushed hull_mid past its print-time ceiling. The ribs are 2.4 mm webs that ramp up to boss width only where a screw lands, and ramp down to a 0.8 mm plinth at the ends so they start on the print bed.

rejected.value: zinc-plated screws
rejected.why: zinc beside brass inserts in fresh water is a rust streak within a season, on the four fasteners that come out every session.

rejected.value: screwing the battery down
rejected.why: a pack swapped every session should not be on threads. It sits between two printed chocks under a hook-and-loop strap, which is also what lets it slide fore and aft to trim the boat.

decisions.summary: Twelve M3 screws into ten brass heat-set inserts, a propeller shaft with a stuffing tube, a propeller, a transom rudder with its stock and tiller, a pushrod in a guide tube, and four wire runs -- all as solids in the assembly rather than numbers in a verdict. Plus a new gate, boat.hull_penetrations, that enumerates every hole through the shell or a watertight bulkhead and refuses more than one below the loaded waterline.
decisions.title: Model the fasteners, the driveline and the wiring as geometry, and gate the hull penetrations

decisions.body:
WHY IT IS AN IMPROVEMENT, not a convenience: a watertight bulkhead printed integral with its hull has no bond line to fail, and watertightness is the top physical risk on this boat (claim P1, one of five only water can settle). Seven glued joints became two.

WHAT IT COST, stated:
* Printed mass 480 g -> 516 g and print time 19.8 h -> 21.3 h. About 10 g of that is not real: overlapping bodies double-count their overlap, which inflates the modelled mass by roughly 2% in the conservative direction. The other ~26 g is: the integral decks are 2.0 mm where the loose panels were 1.4 mm, and the plates now cover the full section and stand 0.3 mm proud instead of being inset.
* An integral bulkhead can no longer be epoxy-filleted from both sides. It does not need to be, because it has no joint, but the hull-to-hull seam beside it is now filleted from one side only.
* hull_mid ships as seven overlapping bodies rather than one solid, and cad.wall_thickness measures 0.24 mm across an internal face between two of them. That gate was already failing before this change, on deck_mid, for the same reason.

Loaded freeboard moved 27.3 mm -> 26.5 mm and trim -1.22 -> -1.27 degrees on the extra 39 g. Both still pass. No claim that passed before this change fails after it.

rejected.value: merging the STEM CAP into hull_bow
rejected.why: at the top of a bulkhead-down print it roofs the open cavity. fdm.bridge_span measured an 85 mm unsupported span across 2649 mm2. Printing that segment stem-down only moves the problem to the bulkhead, which is 132 mm wide rather than 85. It stays a separate 69 x 39 mm plate.

rejected.value: merging the BOW DECK into hull_bow
rejected.why: it prints fine as a longitudinal wall, but hull_bow will not fuse to a single body, and as a separate body inside the same part its underside roofs the cavity with nothing in the same body beneath it: fdm.bridge_span, 19 mm, UNANCHORED. As its own part it lies flat on the bed and the question does not arise. Rejecting it also keeps the bow compartment open until the foam and the interior epoxy are in, and sealed air with no foam fails closed-loop.

rejected.value: putting each bulkhead on the segment it closes
rejected.why: bulkhead_aft belongs to hull_mid and bulkhead_fwd to hull_bow, not to hull_aft and hull_mid. A bulkhead only merges into the segment whose print puts it on the BED.

rejected.value: a boolean union to make each merged part a single solid
rejected.why: attempted, measured and rejected. Blender unions the bodies correctly by volume (0.95-0.98 of the inputs) but the result never survives the normalisation cad-solid applies on load: 2 non-manifold edges and 11 degenerate faces on hull_aft. manifold3d returns a watertight body in milliseconds whose STL round-trip is not watertight. geometry.fuse still tries and its guard still catches it, so the parts ship as overlapping bodies.

decisions.summary: The transom, both bulkheads, the centre girder, the shaft seat and two of the three deck panels stopped being separate parts and are now printed as part of the hull segment they used to be glued to. Each hull segment prints on a transverse face with its one solid cross-wall ON THE BED, which is what makes the merge possible at all: put a cross-wall at the far end of a segment and it becomes a 186 mm horizontal plate at the top of the print.
decisions.title: Merge the loose plates into the hull segments: 13 parts and 8 plates down to 6 and 4

decisions.body: This decision is the reason the part count is thirteen rather than six. Every one of the extra parts is a flat plate that exists so that no hull segment has to roof itself over.

rejected.value: keel down
rejected.why: the hull bottom is near-flat and the keel has rocker, so all but one line of it is an unsupported near-horizontal overhang. Unprintable.

rejected.value: deck down
rejected.why: the same flat bottom, now a roof at the top of the print. Needs support over roughly 200 x 160 mm.

rejected.value: split on the centreline
rejected.why: prints beautifully with zero support and puts a 400 mm glue seam along the keel: underwater, in the highest-stress region, and the single worst place on the boat to have a seam. Rejected on watertightness, claim P1, not on printability.

rejected.value: closed-ended hull segments
rejected.why: a closed tube printed axially has to bridge its own section at one end, which is 160 mm of unsupported span. That is why the transom, both bulkheads and the stem are separate flat plates rather than integral.

decisions.summary: Hull segments print standing on a transverse cut face. The section changes slowly along a hull this slender, so every wall is within about 27 degrees of vertical and nothing needs support. Plates and decks print flat. The exception is hull_bow, which wants about 450 mm2 of support at the stem taper.
decisions.title: Print every part standing on a transverse face or flat; no supports except at the stem

decisions.body: Consequence worth stating: because the solve exists, the battery strap is a design feature. Sliding the battery is the trim adjustment, and boat.trim is what says how far.

rejected.value: install a CFD solver
rejected.why: two gigabytes, an afternoon of setup, a meshing skill, and fifteen minutes a run, to answer a question a page of algebra answers exactly. Static trim is hydrostatics, not fluid dynamics: there is no flow in it. A solver here would be slower, less accurate and unfalsifiable.

rejected.value: use LCG-LCB offset as a proxy and skip the solve
rejected.why: it was the first version and it is a proxy for the thing that matters rather than the thing. The number a builder can act on is the trim ANGLE and the freeboard left after it, and the offset does not give either without the solve.

rejected.value: ignore trim, since three hydrostatic gates were already green
rejected.why: which is the failure the pack warns about by name. On this boat trim costs 3.8 mm of the lowest deck-edge freeboard, 15% of the claim. Level flotation reports 31.1 mm and the boat floats at 27.3 mm.

decisions.summary: fluids-analytic names longitudinal trim as its own nearest omission. Rather than reaching for CFD, the gap is closed in model/hullform.flotation: two unknowns (the waterline height and its slope), two equations (displacement equals mass, centre of buoyancy under centre of gravity), nested bisection, a few milliseconds. It is exactly the sequence docs/EXTENSION_PROTOCOL.md asks for -- name the quantity, classify it, try the analytic answer FIRST, and only reach for a solver if the closed form cannot answer.
decisions.title: Fill the trim gap with closed-form arithmetic, not a solver

decisions.body: FLAG FOR THE USER: this is the one number in the project that is purely my invention. If 400 USD is wrong, change budget_usd in model/boat.py and re-run; bom.cost will tell you what has to go. The 374.50 USD also carries +/-25%: Amazon refused every product-page fetch during sourcing, so only eight of nineteen lines have a price verified on a fetchable page.

rejected.value: 200 USD, by cutting parts
rejected.why: the three lines that would have to go are the ones the engineering depends on. The RC4WD 80-turn motor (22 USD) is 12 USD dearer than a stock 380 and is the whole reason the propeller turns at 4450 rpm instead of 22000. The Savox IP67 servo (40 USD) is 34 USD dearer than an MG90S and is the one component guaranteed to meet water. The Flysky set (54 USD) has no cheaper credible alternative. Cutting them buys 80 USD and costs the boat.

rejected.value: leave the budget at 200 and report the overrun
rejected.why: the budget is a claim in the ledger, and a claim nobody intends to meet is noise in every future sweep. Either it moves with a reason or it is not a budget.

decisions.summary: The 200 USD budget was mine, not the user s: the brief said Amazon-orderable and beginner-friendly and never named a number. With real prices for parts that meet the specs, the bill is 374.50 USD. bom.cost failed against 200 and that failure is the reason this decision exists rather than a number quietly edited into the model.
decisions.title: Raise the build budget from 200 to 400 USD

decisions.body: Every one of these came out of packs/fluids-analytic/lenses.md, run before any geometry existed. None of it would have shown up in a gate sweep, because fluid.metacentric reports solid GM and has no concept of a compartment.

rejected.value: one open hull interior
rejected.why: the free-surface correction on an undivided 163 mm wide bilge is i/V = 278 mm against a solid GM of 74 mm. Three millimetres of water in the bilge and the boat is upside down. This is not a margin problem, it is a sign problem.

rejected.value: transverse bulkheads only, no centre girder
rejected.why: free-surface second moment is L*b^3/12: transverse bulkheads cut L, which is LINEAR, while a longitudinal division cuts b, which is CUBIC. One centre girder divides the effect by four; three transverse bulkheads divide it by three at ten times the cost in mass and print time.

rejected.value: sealed air compartments with no foam
rejected.why: fluids lens 5: sealed air volumes fail closed-loop. One crack in a printed bow compartment and the entire reserve buoyancy is gone at the moment it is needed. Closed-cell foam fails gracefully and costs about two dollars of pool noodle.

rejected.value: a bilge pump
rejected.why: an order of magnitude more cost, mass, current and failure modes than a bulkhead, and it does nothing about free surface while it is pumping.

decisions.summary: The equipment bay is bounded by two watertight transverse bulkheads, leaving a sealed bow compartment and a sealed stern compartment. A longitudinal centre girder runs the length of the equipment bay bilge, dividing it into two half-width cells. Both sealed end compartments are filled with closed-cell foam.
decisions.title: Three compartments, a longitudinal centre girder, and closed-cell foam in the ends

decisions.body: Displacement scales as s^3 and printed shell mass as roughly s^2, while motor, ESC, servo, receiver and battery do not scale at all. That is the whole argument: going up in size is the cheapest way to buy freeboard on a boat whose payload is fixed by what you can buy. The cost is filament and print hours, both of which the fdm gates will price.

rejected.value: 1.00 (LOA 300 mm as drawn)
rejected.why: displaces 73 g at the drawn DWL and about 400 g at 23 mm draft, which leaves ~15 mm of freeboard with a +/-15% mass estimate riding on it. It floats, but C2 (25 mm freeboard) fails and there is no margin for the mass estimate being wrong. Also does not fit a 220 mm bed in one piece anyway, so it does not even buy a single-piece print.

hull halves come out 225 mm long and no longer fit a 220x220 bed, which breaks the "buildable at home" constraint for the most common printer class. 1.40 gives 210 mm halves, which fit with 10 mm to spare.

rejected.value: keep LOA 300 and cut mass instead
rejected.why: the floor is real: the smallest usable 2S pack is ~75 g, a 370-class motor ~55 g, and the printed shell scales with surface area not with wishes. ~390 g is the floor and it still leaves 15 mm of freeboard.

rejected.value: redraw the hull deeper at LOA 300
rejected.why: the user said they like this hull profile. Changing the form is a bigger change than changing the scale, and it throws away the one piece of evidence the project has.

decisions.summary: The hull as drawn at LOA 300 mm displaces 73 g at the waterline the design tool drew. The parts alone are ~265 g and the printed shell another ~130 g, so the drawn waterline is a styling line, not a loading condition. Scaling the traced offsets by 1.40 (LOA 420 mm, deck beam 163 mm, depth 65.5 mm) buys displacement as the cube of scale while the electronics mass stays fixed, and lands the loaded waterline at roughly 20 mm draft in a 65.5 mm deep hull. The hull FORM is unchanged: every offset is the traced one times 1.40, so the boat the user liked is the boat they get, bigger.
decisions.title: Scale the traced hull to LOA 420 mm; keep the shape exactly

inputs.description: Hull-design tool screenshot: profile, plan, body-plan and section views of a 300 mm displacement hull with transom stern. Reports LOA 300, unit mm, WL slider 44.20, rake 0.0 deg, and a section cut at x=150 mm with draft 8.14 and WL beam 76.24.

extractions.note: Panels were mis-identified on the first pass (plan vs profile are swapped from the intuitive layout); the DWL in the profile panel is dead horizontal at y=1547 px and that is the tell. Recorded in tools/trace_hull_profile.py.
extractions.what: Toolbar reads LOA 300, Unit mm, WL slider 44.20, Rake 0.0 deg. The CUT panel reads "x=150 mm, draft 8.14, WL beam 76.24". Pixel-tracing the three panels (tools/trace_hull_profile.py) recovers the full lines plan at ~0.235 mm/px: LOA 300 mm, max deck beam 116.4 mm, max hull depth 46.8 mm sheer-to-keel, max DWL beam 83.2 mm, deepest keel 8.40 mm below the drawn DWL. Section at x=150 is a flat-bottomed hard-bilge form with near-vertical flared topsides. Three INDEPENDENT scale estimates (CUT y from draft 8.14, CUT x from WL beam 76.24, profile x from LOA 300) agree to 2.1%, so the trace and the tool report the same hull.

extractions.note: This is the single finding that changes the design. It is why hull_scale exists as a parameter.
extractions.what: CONSEQUENCE, computed from the trace: integrating the traced sections, the hull AS DRAWN at LOA 300 mm displaces only 73 g at the waterline the tool drew (draft 8.40 mm). A realistic parts list for this boat (motor, ESC, servo, receiver, 2S LiPo, driveline, rudder) is ~265 g before any printed structure, and the printed hull is another ~130 g. The drawn waterline is therefore a styling waterline, not a loading condition, and the hull at LOA 300 has no usable freeboard margin once loaded.

params.name: hull_scale
params.rationale: Multiplier on every traced offset. THE decision of this project. At 1.00 (the LOA 300 mm the design tool reported) the hull displaces 73 g at the waterline the tool drew, and about 477 g of boat would float it with 10 mm of freeboard -- a fail on C2 with a +/-15% mass estimate riding on it. Displacement goes as scale^3 while motor, ESC, servo, receiver and battery do not scale at all, so scale is the cheapest freeboard there is. 1.50 was rejected: 225 mm hull segments no longer fit a 220 x 220 bed. 1.40 gives 210 mm segments with room for a brim. See `atompipe why hull_scale`.

params.name: traced_loa_mm
params.rationale: LOA the design tool reported, and the length every traced offset is in.

params.name: wall_mm
params.rationale: Hull shell wall. 4 perimeters at a 0.4 mm nozzle. 1.2 mm (3 perimeters) is the printable minimum and is what C8 asks for, but the hull shell is the pressure boundary and 1.2 mm PETG has visible pinholes at the layer bonds on a curved wall. 2.0 mm was tried and costs 55 g for stiffness nothing needs.

params.name: deck_mm
params.rationale: Deck panels. Not a pressure boundary and not loaded; 2.4 mm cost 46 g across the three panels and the hatch for nothing. 1.2 mm was tried next, on the reasoning that 3 perimeters at a 0.4 mm nozzle is 1.2 mm, and fdm.min_wall refused it: thinnest section 1.20 mm = 2.6 beads vs 1.38 mm minimum (3 x 0.46 mm line width) Three perimeters is three EXTRUSION WIDTHS, not three nozzle diameters, and the extrusion width is about 1.15x the nozzle. 1.4 mm is three real beads.

params.name: plate_mm
params.rationale: Transom and bulkhead plates. These ARE loaded (the bulkheads are what stops the hull folding, and the transom carries the rudder bracket) so they are thicker than the deck and thinner than the shell, which only has to be thick because it has to be watertight.

params.name: hatch_mm
params.rationale: Hatch lid plate. Same 3-bead minimum as the deck; it is handled and occasionally leaned on, so it is not thinner than the deck it sits on.

params.name: hatch_lip_mm
params.rationale: Depth the lid's rails drop into the opening. Deep enough to locate the lid positively when the tape is compressed, shallow enough that you can lift it out with wet fingers.

params.name: hatch_land_mm
params.rationale: How far the lid overhangs the coaming on every side. It is the gasket land: the foam tape sits under this, so it has to be wider than the tape.

params.name: coaming_w_mm
params.rationale: Width of the raised rim around the hatch opening, AWAY FROM the hatch screws. It grows to boss width (4.6 mm of insert plus 2 mm of wall each side) only in the four short zones where a screw lands -- see coaming_boss_half_mm. The coaming IS the boss, which is why this boat has no separate boss posts. In this print orientation a post standing off the deck is a cylinder cantilevered horizontally off a wall and its underside needs support; a rib running along the hull's x axis is a vertical wall in the print and needs none. Carrying boss width for all 186 mm of it, though, was 8 g of plastic to hold four screws.

params.name: coaming_boss_half_mm
params.rationale: Half-length of the widened zone around each hatch screw.

params.name: coaming_h_mm
params.rationale: A raised lip around the hatch opening. Water on deck runs round it instead of into the equipment bay. Four millimetres is enough for a pond and is one layer of overhang at the top, not a bridge.

params.name: lip_wall_mm
params.rationale: Wall of every printed rail and rim. 5 beads at a 0.4 nozzle: these are short unsupported walls and 2 mm prints reliably where 1.2 mm wanders.

params.name: plate_lip_inset_mm
params.rationale: Vestigial: the plates no longer carry locating lips (see make_parts). Kept so a future variant that wants them does not have to re-derive the inset.

params.name: spigot_mm
params.rationale: Length a locating feature projects across a joint. Now only used as the lip length the bulkheads would have had; see make_parts for why the lips went.

params.name: spigot_wall_mm
params.rationale: Wall of a projecting locating ring. Vestigial with the lips; see make_parts.

params.name: fit_clearance_mm
params.rationale: Clearance on every printed plug fit. 0.2 is the usual FDM number and it is too tight here: these are large, curved, thin-walled mouldings that come off the bed 0.3 mm out of round, and a spigot you have to force into a hull is a spigot that cracks it.

params.name: body_overlap_mm
params.rationale: How far every sub-body pokes into its neighbour instead of abutting it. Face-coincident bodies are watertight in memory and stop being watertight the moment they go through STL, which has no vertex identity: the loader welds the duplicated vertices and the shared face becomes a seam of non-manifold edges. 0.08 mm is a fifth of a nozzle -- invisible to a slicer, and no shared vertices to weld.

params.name: merge_bite_mm
params.rationale: How far an integral feature -- a bulkhead, the transom, the deck, the girder, the shaft seat -- sinks into the hull segment it is part of. It is not a clearance, it is the opposite: geometry.fuse unions the bodies into one solid, and a boolean union of bodies that merely TOUCH is a no-op that looks exactly like a successful merge (same body count, same volume). 0.6 mm is a third of the wall, enough to be unambiguous to a boolean and invisible in the result.

params.name: coaming_set_in_mm
params.rationale: Where the coaming's inboard face sits relative to the hatch opening's edge. NEGATIVE, i.e. 0.3 mm outboard of it. Two things have to be true at once: it must not be coplanar with the deck rail's edge (a shared face there welds on STL load and the part stops being watertight), and it must clear the lid's rails, which drop into the opening at fit_clearance. At +0.4 it did neither -- the coaming's face sat 0.05 mm proud of where the lid's rail wanted to be, and cad.clash found 135 mm3 of hatch_cover inside hull_mid.

params.name: plate_proud_mm
params.rationale: How far a transom, bulkhead or stem plate stands past the hull's outer skin. Proud rather than inset, so the hull tube's end ring lands entirely ON the plate instead of half on nothing, and so no ray can travel along a rim of bare wall beside it. It doubles as a register for the segment that butts against it.

params.name: insert_od_mm
params.rationale: Outside diameter of an M3 brass heat-set insert, standard short pattern. It is what sets every boss bore and therefore every boss diameter, so it is in docs/BUY.md beside the part: buy a different insert and the bosses are wrong.

params.name: insert_len_mm
params.rationale: Length of the same insert. Every boss carries at least this much blind depth plus a millimetre, which is why the coaming is 9 mm wide and not 5.

params.name: screw_head_h_mm
params.rationale: M3 pan head. STAINLESS or nylon, never zinc-plated: zinc plating in fresh water with dissimilar metals around it is a rust streak within a season, and the screws that matter here are the four you undo every time you change the battery.

params.name: boss_wall_mm
params.rationale: Material around an insert. Below about 1.5 mm the boss splits when the insert goes in hot; 2 mm is five extrusion widths.

params.name: hatch_screw_n
params.rationale: Four, at the corners of the hatch. Two would let the middle of a 200 mm lid lift off its gasket; six is four more holes in the only part that has to seal.

params.name: mount_web_mm
params.rationale: Thickness of a mounting rib away from its bosses. Six extrusion widths, which is a web, not a wall. Carrying full boss width down the whole rib cost 13 cm3 per rib to hold two M3 screws, and three of those ribs pushed hull_mid's print time past its 14 h ceiling.

params.name: boss_pad_mm
params.rationale: Side of the local square pad that thickens a rib to boss width around one insert. Big enough for 4.6 mm of insert plus 2 mm of wall plus somewhere to put the drill.

params.name: pushrod_shortfall_mm
params.rationale: FIXTURE KNOB: how far the pushrod's aft end stops short of the tiller. Zero in the design. boat.linkage_closed's negative control sets it to 6 mm, which is a clevis on the wrong hole -- and is what the boat actually had, unnoticed, for a whole revision.

params.name: max_mating_gap_mm
params.rationale: How far apart two consecutive members of a drive or steering chain may be before they are not connected. Every pair in the design is at 0.00 mm -- they interpenetrate, because that is what a shaft in a coupler or a stock in a bearing does -- so 1 mm is not a tolerance being used up, it is the width of the band in which a modelling slip is still recoverable. See boat.linkage_closed.

params.name: max_below_waterline_penetrations
params.rationale: How many holes through the shell below the loaded waterline this design is allowed. ONE: the propeller shaft, which is unavoidable because the propeller has to be driven from inside. Everything else -- the pushrod, the rudder bracket, the switch rod -- is routed above the waterline for exactly this reason, and boat.hull_penetrations is what stops that drifting. A boss that migrates below the waterline during a later edit is a leak nobody decided to make.

params.name: seat_side_clear_mm
params.rationale: Gap the shaft seat leaves to the hull's inner surface on each side. The seat is clamped to the cavity width at its own height, and this is what it leaves for the epoxy fillet that bonds it in.

params.name: merge_inset_mm
params.rationale: How far an integral deck's outboard edge stops short of the hull's outer skin. Flush is worse than either proud or inset: it hands the boolean a pair of exactly coplanar vertical faces running the whole length of the part, and what comes back is a single body that is not watertight.

params.name: deck_lap_mm
params.rationale: How far deck sub-panels lap each other. It has to EXCEED the minimum wall, because the lap is a wall: at 0.08 mm the lap was a 0.16 mm slab and cad.wall_thickness correctly reported a 0.160 mm section through it.

params.name: deck_step_mm
params.rationale: Vertical step between lapped deck sub-panels, so their faces are never coincident. See geometry.deck_panel. Under a fifth of a layer: the slicer never sees it.

params.name: gasket_mm
params.rationale: Compressed thickness of the closed-cell foam tape between the coaming's top face and the underside of the hatch lid. It is a real part on the BOM, and modelling it as a gap is also what stops the lid and the coaming reading as 5541 mm3 of interference.

params.name: deck_gap_mm
params.rationale: Epoxy bond line between the hull/bulkhead tops and the underside of the deck. Also the thing that keeps those faces from being exactly coplanar, which a boolean engine cannot answer questions about -- see geometry.deck_panel.

params.name: tip_clear_mm
params.rationale: How far the blunt stem is held BELOW the flat deck. Without it the traced sheer at the stem rises past deck_z, the vertical strake collapses to its 0.05 mm minimum, and cad.wall_thickness casts a ray into the resulting sliver.

params.name: tip_half_beam_mm
params.rationale: Half the width of the blunt stem face. A hull tapering to a mathematical point is unprintable (nothing is narrower than one extrusion width) and unmeasurable: cad.wall_thickness reported a 0.003 mm wall into the old knife edge. 4 mm across the stem is ten beads and invisible on a 480 mm boat.

params.name: tip_depth_mm
params.rationale: Height of the blunt stem face. Same reason as tip_half_beam_mm; together they make the stem a real face the stem plate can be bonded to.

params.name: min_cavity_mm
params.rationale: The hull tube stops where its internal cavity narrows to this. It is a PRINTABILITY number, not a structural one: past this point the inward offset self-intersects, and the solid nose that used to fill the gap failed cad.wall_thickness, fdm.overhang and fdm.bridge_span in turn depending on which way up it was printed. 25 mm truncates the stem by about 5 mm and replaces all three failures with one more flat plate.

params.name: section_points
params.rationale: Points per half-section. 24 puts about 4 mm between points at the turn of bilge, which is where this hull has all its curvature. 12 visibly facets the bilge; 48 doubles the mesh for a difference no slicer resolves.

params.name: mesh_dx_mm
params.rationale: Longitudinal station spacing in the generated mesh. 5 mm. The hull changes slowly along x, so this is about surface quality rather than accuracy.

params.name: girder_t_mm
params.rationale: Girder web thickness. 6 beads. It is a bonded web in shear, not a column.

params.name: girder_h_mm
params.rationale: Longitudinal centre girder in the equipment bay bilge. Its job is FREE SURFACE, not strength: bilge-water free-surface inertia goes as L*b^3/12, so halving the bilge width divides the effect by four, while a transverse bulkhead only cuts L and does so linearly. 10 mm, reduced from 18. cad.clash found the 18 mm web occupying the same space as the battery (2465 mm3, 2.1 mm deep) and the motor (630 mm3) -- all three live on the centreline and nobody had noticed. Ten millimetres clears both, and it still divides the bilge where bilge water actually sits: water deeper than 10 mm across this bay is 300 g aboard and an emergency rather than a stability nuance. The battery now sits ON the girder and straddles it, which is a better fit than the original anyway. See the decision log.

params.name: bulkhead_aft_x
params.rationale: Aft watertight bulkhead. Set by THREE things at once: it is the aft end of the equipment bay, it is a print split, and it is the boundary of the sealed aft compartment that boat.swamped depends on. It was at 110 mm and moved to 150 mm when the swamped margin came out at -7 g: moving both bulkheads inward buys sealed volume at both ends and cost 25 mm of bay length.

params.name: bulkhead_fwd_x
params.rationale: The two watertight bulkheads. They bound the equipment bay and they are also the print splits, which is not a coincidence: a seam at a bulkhead gets a plate glued across it, and a seam in open shell gets a butt joint and a prayer.

params.name: hatch_x0
params.rationale: Forward and aft ends of the hatch opening, and its half width. Sized to get the motor (50 mm long, 35.5 mm diameter) and the battery in and out with the deck on, and inset from the bulkheads far enough to leave a gasket land all round.

params.name: hatch_x1
params.rationale: See hatch_x0.

params.name: hatch_half_w
params.rationale: See hatch_x0. Also bounded by the coaming needing to land on deck inboard of the hull's topsides.

params.name: tube_od_mm
params.rationale: Stuffing tube OD, from the uxcell kit on the BOM. The hull is drilled 10.2 mm to leave room for the epoxy fillet that is the actual seal.

params.name: tube_outboard_x_mm
params.rationale: Where the stuffing tube starts and ends along the shaft axis. Inboard it stops just forward of the aft bulkhead it passes through; outboard it stops short of the propeller so the shaft runs in water for the last 12 mm, which is what the kit's outer bearing expects.

params.name: rudder_blade_top_mm
params.rationale: Top of the rudder blade, just above the keel datum. The stock runs from the BOTTOM of the blade up through the bracket's bore to the tiller, so blade, stock and tiller are one connected assembly rather than three solids near each other.

params.name: rudder_bracket_lwh_mm
params.rationale: The transom bracket the rudder hangs from, as a solid. Its hole spacing is NOT published by the vendor -- measure the bracket you actually get before drilling the transom, because those two holes are hull penetrations.

params.name: pushrod_z_mm
params.rationale: Height of the pushrod run above the keel. It is 22 mm ABOVE the loaded waterline, and that is the whole reason it is at this height: the pushrod tube pierces both the aft bulkhead and the transom, and a penetration above the waterline is a different kind of risk from one below it. boat.hull_penetrations is the gate that will not let this drift.

params.name: wire_d_mm
params.rationale: Representative diameter for a routed pair of silicone wires. Not a spec: it is there so cad.clash can see that the runs have somewhere to go that is not across the propeller shaft.

params.name: shaft_exit_x_mm
params.rationale: Where the stuffing tube leaves the hull bottom. Forward enough that the tube has a long bonded run inside the sealed aft compartment, aft enough that the shaft line does not have to be steep to clear the motor. boat.driveline settles it.

params.name: shaft_angle_deg
params.rationale: Down-aft angle of the propeller shaft. 8-12 degrees is the practical band: a flexible coupler will not take much more, and a shallower angle puts the motor on the hull floor. 15 degrees was tried to gain motor clearance and pushes the thrust line far enough off horizontal to trim the boat by the stern under power.

params.name: prop_x_mm
params.rationale: Propeller centre, aft of the transom. Aft, not under the hull, and that is forced rather than chosen: this hull draws 30 mm and a 35 mm propeller under it would need a skeg deeper than the boat. Aft of the transom the hull does not constrain the disc at all, which is also why the rudder has to be transom-mounted.

params.name: prop_dia_mm
params.rationale: 35 mm, which is what the brass scale propeller on the BOM is. It sets how deep the propeller hangs (tip 20 mm below the keel) and therefore the prop-to-hull and prop-to-rudder clearances boat.driveline checks.

params.name: rudder_x_mm
params.rationale: Rudder pivot, aft of the transom. Set by the propeller: the blade has to be in the wash and clear of the disc, which boat.driveline enforces at 10 mm minimum. Anything further aft is a longer unsupported bracket for no gain.

params.name: rudder_depth_mm
params.rationale: Blade depth below the keel datum. Rudder area wants roughly 1.25 square inches per foot of boat, which is about 1550 mm2 here, and the area scales with the square of speed - this boat is slow, so the rudder is deliberately oversized.

params.name: rudder_chord_mm
params.rationale: Blade chord. With the depth, this is what sets the area; deep-and-narrow beats wide-and-shallow for authority at low speed.

params.name: shaft_block_len_mm
params.rationale: The internal block the stuffing tube is bonded through. Long enough to give the tube a real bearing length rather than a point, which is what stops the tube working loose and starting a leak at the one penetration below the waterline.

params.name: shaft_block_w_mm
params.rationale: See shaft_block_len_mm. Wide enough to take a 9.5 mm tube with wall either side.

params.name: shaft_block_h_mm
params.rationale: See shaft_block_len_mm.

params.name: min_prop_tip_clearance_mm
params.rationale: Minimum gap from the propeller disc to any part of the hull. Below about 8 mm the blade tips work in the hull's boundary layer, which is noise, vibration and lost thrust.

params.name: min_prop_rudder_gap_mm
params.rationale: Minimum gap from the propeller disc to the rudder leading edge. Too close and the rudder sits in the blade wake and hammers; too far and it is out of the wash and the boat will not turn at low speed.

params.name: max_shaft_angle_deg
params.rationale: What a flexible coupler will take without eating its own bearings. 12 degrees is the practical ceiling quoted for these universal joints.

params.name: place
params.rationale: Where each component sits, as (x, y, z) of its box centre. z = None means "on the shaft axis" for the motor and "on the hull floor" for anything else on the centreline. ANYTHING OFF THE CENTRELINE NEEDS AN EXPLICIT z. This hull's sections pinch hard at the turn of bilge -- the half-beam is 21% of maximum at 3% of the depth above the keel -- so a box placed off-centre at floor level has its outboard bottom corner outside the hull. cad.clash caught exactly that on the first layout. The battery's x is also the trim adjustment, which is why it is strapped rather than glued: sliding it changes LCG, and boat.trim is the gate that says how far.

params.name: floor_standoff_mm
params.rationale: Everything on the hull floor sits on 2 mm of standoff. Anything resting directly in the bilge is sitting in the first millilitre of water that gets in.

params.name: mass_contingency_frac
params.rationale: 8% on top of the itemised mass, for glue, sealant, paint, wire, solder, the hook-and-loop strap and the water an FDM hull absorbs. First builds run 10-20% over the paper mass; 8% is the part of that which is not already itemised.

params.name: design_speed_m_s
params.rationale: Froude 0.39 at this waterline length. fluids-analytic computes no wave-making resistance and says so, and becomes a statement about a boat at rest above Froude 0.4. Choosing 0.8 keeps C5 inside the pack's stated validity envelope rather than outside it. 1.2 m/s was the first number and is Froude 0.59 -- past hull speed, where the drag verdict would have been arithmetic about nothing.

params.name: thrust_available_n
params.rationale: Static thrust of a 35 mm 3-blade on a 380 at 7.4 V. CLASS FIGURE, not measured, and the weakest number in the drag chain -- see the readiness report.

params.name: hull_cd
params.rationale: Drag coefficient on FRONTAL area (the immersed midship section). The pack's table is frontal-referenced and its lens list calls out using a planform or wetted-area Cd with a frontal area as a factor-of-several error with no symptom. 0.11 is a slender streamlined body at Re ~3e5.

params.name: heel_angle_deg
params.rationale: fluid.righting_arm has NO default heel and skips without one, because GZ is a function of the angle and a gate that picked one would be choosing the load case. 8 degrees, not 10: 10 is exactly the small-angle ceiling, which is the largest arm the gate can ever report.

params.name: max_volume_fraction
params.rationale: C1. The pack default is 0.90, which is a hull floating almost awash. A pond boat gets rained on, takes spray over the transom and leaks a little at the shaft; 0.55 leaves 45% of the moulded volume as reserve.

params.name: min_freeboard_limit_mm
params.rationale: Named `..._limit_mm` rather than `min_freeboard_mm` because the first version used one name for the THRESHOLD here and for the MEASURED value out of build(), and `atompipe check` refused to let that slide: warning: model and build() disagree on min_freeboard_mm: config 25.0 vs build() 31.81 - gates read the config value A gate comparing against 25.0 while the report printed 31.8 would have been a silent inconsistency in the reassuring direction, which is the kind that survives review. 25 mm itself is a project judgement, well above the pack default of 15% of hull depth (12.3 mm here), set by pond chop and by the deck edge being where water gets in.

params.name: min_gm_mm
params.rationale: C3. The pack default is 5% of waterline beam, which is 7.4 mm here. KG is an estimate rather than a weighed number, so the default leaves no room for the estimate being wrong. 15 mm is about 10% of waterline beam.

params.name: min_gz_mm
params.rationale: C4. The righting arm at 8 degrees. Covers a one-sided load - the whole battery adrift against one side of the bay, or a hand shoving the boat off a dock.

params.name: min_gm_free_surface_mm
params.rationale: C17 and C19. GM after the bilge free-surface correction, and GM empty. Lower than min_gm_mm on purpose: these are degraded conditions and the question is whether the boat is still stable, not whether it is still comfortable.

params.name: max_trim_deg
params.rationale: Trim angle, either way. 1.5 degrees on this hull costs about 5 mm of the lowest deck-edge freeboard, which is a fifth of the freeboard claim -- that is the scale at which trim stops being cosmetic. It is set by what a movable battery can actually correct, not by comfort: there is nobody aboard.

params.name: max_lcg_lcb_offset_mm
params.rationale: Secondary to max_trim_deg, which is the claim that has teeth. Kept because the offset is the number you can act on: it says how far to slide the battery.

params.name: max_mass_budget_error_frac
params.rationale: Vestigial: the mass-budget claim was replaced by boat.wall_agreement after the original version turned out to be a tautology. See claim C14.

params.name: envelope_x_mm
params.rationale: Longest dimension of the assembled boat, boxed: a car boot and a kitchen table. It also catches a units slip, because a model that has silently gone metres-for-millimetres fails boat.envelope loudly instead of exporting a plausible STL that nobody measures.

params.name: envelope_y_mm
params.rationale: Width of the same envelope, with the rudder and prop shaft off.

params.name: envelope_z_mm
params.rationale: Height of the same envelope, measured over the coaming and the hatch.

params.name: max_moq_overbuy_usd
params.rationale: Amazon MOQ is normally 1, so this should be trivially green. That is the point: it is a cheap gate that would catch the one line that quietly is not.

params.name: max_lead_days
params.rationale: Three weeks. Anything longer is not "order it on Amazon this evening", which is the constraint the brief actually set.

params.name: budget_usd
params.rationale: Total parts cost, excluding the printer. THIS IS THE ONE NUMBER IN THE PROJECT THAT IS PURELY INVENTED: the brief said Amazon-orderable and beginner-friendly and never named a figure. It started at 200, bom.cost failed at 374.50 against real prices, and it was raised with the alternatives written down rather than quietly edited - see `atompipe why budget_usd`. Change it, re-run, and bom.cost will say what has to go.

params.name: material
params.rationale: PETG. PLA absorbs water, creeps, and goes brittle; a PLA hull left in a hot car delaminates at the layer lines, which on a boat is the failure that matters, and its heat-deflection temperature is around 55 C against a 50 C dark-plastic surface in sun. ASA would be better still and does not print on an open frame without warping a 190 mm part.

params.name: nozzle_mm
params.rationale: 0.4 mm. Every wall thickness in this model is a whole number of beads at this nozzle; change it and min_wall, deck_mm and lip_wall_mm all move.

params.name: layer_mm
params.rationale: 0.24 mm, 60% of the nozzle. Measured work on printed watertightness puts 0.15 mm best and 0.3 mm worst; 0.24 is the compromise that keeps a 190 mm part under seven hours. Drop it to 0.15 for the hull segments if the leak test finds seams.

params.name: perimeters
params.rationale: 4. Measured leak testing puts PETG at 4 perimeters to be watertight UNTREATED. This build also epoxy-coats the interior, so 4 is belt and braces on the one thing that cannot be fixed after assembly.

params.name: infill_frac
params.rationale: 15%. Nearly irrelevant to a thin-shelled hull - perimeter count is the dominant mass variable, not infill - but it matters for the plates.

params.name: print_speed_mm_s
params.rationale: 60 mm/s. Conservative, because the tall standing hull segments are the shape most likely to ring or knock over.

params.name: bed_x_mm
params.rationale: 220 x 220 x 250 mm: the Ender-3 / Prusa-Mini class machine most people who would build this actually own. Every print split in the model is set by it.

params.name: bed_y_mm
params.rationale: See bed_x_mm.

params.name: bed_z_mm
params.rationale: See bed_x_mm. Not binding: the tallest part is hull_mid at 190 mm.

params.name: brim_mm
params.rationale: 6 mm of brim allowance per side. The tall standing hull segments have a small footprint for their height and want a brim; a part sized to the raw bed does not fit the bed once the brim is on it.

params.name: max_print_time_h
params.rationale: Per-part ceiling. A part that takes longer than an evening is a part you will not reprint when it fails, and on a first build something always fails. RAISED from 14 h to 17 h when the mounting features went in, and it is worth being clear about what kind of number moved. The overhang allowance relaxed earlier in this project protected a PHYSICAL property -- whether the part needs support -- and it went back to the pack default as soon as the geometry allowed. This one is a judgement about the builder's patience. hull_mid is a 190 mm tall, 186 mm wide thin-walled hull section carrying a bulkhead, two deck rails, two coamings, a girder and five mounting ribs; 15.5 h is simply what that costs, and the alternative -- splitting it -- would add a part and a glued joint to a boat whose part count was just halved for watertightness reasons. It is an overnight print, which is normal for a printed hull and is what every published build of this kind does.

params.name: shell_pack_frac
params.rationale: Printed shells (the hull tubes) are modelled at their true wall thickness, so the slicer prints them essentially solid: their mesh volume IS their filament volume. Plates and decks are modelled as solid slabs and DO get infill -- see `plate_pack_frac`. Getting this backwards is a 2x error on the mass that every hydrostatic number depends on, which is why C14 exists.

params.name: plate_pack_frac
params.rationale: A 1.6-2.0 mm slab at 4 perimeters and 0.24 mm layers is mostly perimeter and solid top/bottom skin; the infill setting barely gets a look in. 0.88, not the 0.15 infill figure.

params.name: boolean_merge
params.rationale: Whether to run geometry.fuse over each merged part's bodies. ON, because the alternative does not survive the mesh gates. Each hull segment is built from several deliberately OVERLAPPING closed bodies -- the tube, its transom or bulkhead, its deck, its girder, its shaft seat -- and a slicer would union those quite happily. The gates will not: a multi-body part has INTERNAL faces, and neither cad.wall_thickness nor fdm.bridge_span can tell an internal face from a void. Left unmerged they reported a 0.002 mm wall through 1.6 mm of plastic and a 157 mm unsupported ceiling sitting directly on a bulkhead. Getting the union to work took four findings, all of them recorded in geometry.fuse: union the original body list rather than a re-split concatenation; make the bodies genuinely overlap; use Blender rather than manifold3d; and do almost nothing to the output afterwards -- fill_holes and nothing else, because the obvious cleanup turns 18 open edges into 412. hull_aft and hull_bow come out as single solids. hull_mid does NOT and ships as seven overlapping bodies: its two deck rails and two coamings share end planes with the tube and the bulkhead, and the union comes back with 12 open edges. The guard catches that and hands back the concatenation, which is why one gate is still red against it. That is the honest state, not a rounding of it.

params.name: write_meshes
params.rationale: Whether build() exports STLs. The negative-control fixtures turn it off: they rebuild the model dozens of times and have no use for the files.

params.name: topside_mass_g
params.rationale: Mass added ON TOP of the deck -- a camera mast, a light bar, a superstructure. Zero in the design. The fluids lens list is blunt about why this is the lever that matters: "Additions go UP, almost always, because that is where the space is." The free-surface and empty-condition controls SOLVE for the value that misses their acceptance by 1.15x, rather than typing a number that stops being a control the moment somebody relaxes a threshold.

params.name: topside_z_mm
params.rationale: Height above the keel datum of `topside_mass_g`. 140 mm is roughly a 60 mm mast above an 82 mm hull.

params.name: mesh_wall_scale
params.rationale: FIXTURE KNOB: multiplies the wall used for the INNER offset only, so the generated mesh's wall stops matching the specified wall. 1.0 always, except in boat.wall_agreement's negative control, where 0.5 simulates exactly the class of generator bug this project hit twice.
